Instead of גּם־זה, neut. by attraction, there is here the immediately neut. גּם־זה; the book uniformly makes use of this fem. form instead of זאת. This or that is “in the hand of God,” <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, it is His gift, <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.13">Ecc 3:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.18">Ecc 3:18</reference>, and it is thus conditioned by Him, since man cannot give it to himself; cf. minni, <reference osisRef="Isa.30.1">Isa 30:1</reference>; mimmenni, Hos 8:4; mimmennu, 1Ki 20:33. <div eID="gen12234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12235" type="x-p"/> This dependence of the enjoyment of life on God is established.
entries.e37592b7ef213fa2f9392f121a7e0350baa0fee9: <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.25">Ecc 2:25</reference> “For who can eat, and who can have enjoyment, without [= except from Him?]” Also here the traditional text is tenable: we have to read ממנו חוץ, after the lxx (which Jerome follows in his <hi type="italic">Comm</hi>.) and the Syr. If we adopt the text as it lies before us, then the meaning would be, as given by Gumpel,<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., regarding his noteworthy <hi type="italic">Comm</hi>. on Koheleth, my <hi type="italic">Jesurun</hi>, pp. 183 and 195. The author bears the name among Christians of Professor Levisohn.</note> and thus translated by Jerome: <hi type="italic">Quis ita devorabit et deliciis effluet ut ego?</hi> But (1) the question thus understood would require ממּנּי יותר, which Gumpel and others silently substitute in place of חוץ ם; (2) this question, in which the king adjudicates to himself an unparalleled right to eat and to enjoy himself, would stand out of connection with that which precedes and follows. <div eID="gen12235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12236" type="x-p"/> Even though with Ginsburg, after Rashi, Aben Ezra, and Rashbam, we find in <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.25">Ecc 2:25</reference> the thought that the labourer has the first and nearest title to the enjoyment of the fruit of his labour (חוץ ם thus exemplif. as <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.8">Ecc 4:8</reference>, ע ... למי), the continuation with כּי, <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.26">Ecc 2:26</reference>, is unsuitable; for the natural sequence of the thoughts would then be this: But the enjoyment, far from being connected with the labour as its self-consequence and fruit, is a gift of God, which He gives to one and withholds from another. If we read ממּנּוּ, then the sequence of the thoughts wants nothing in syllogistic exactness. חוּשׁ .ssen here has nothing in common with חוּשׁ = Arab. ḥât, to proceed with a violent, impetuous motion, but, as at <reference osisRef="Job.20.2">Job 20:2</reference>, is = Arab. ḥss, <hi type="italic">stringere</hi> (whence hiss, a sensible impression); the experience here meant is one mediated by means of a pleasant external enjoyment. The lxx, Theod., and Syr. translate: (and who can) drink, which Ewald approves of, for he compares (Arab.) ḥasa (<hi type="italic">inf</hi>. ḥasy), to drink, to sip. But this Arab. verb is unheard of in Heb.; with right, Heiligst. adheres to the Arab., and at the same time the modern Heb. ḥass, חושׁ, <hi type="italic">sentire</hi>, according to which Schultens, <hi type="italic">quis sensibus indulserit</hi>. ממנו חוּץ is not = ולא ם, “except from him” (Hitz., Zöckl.), but מן חוץ together mean “except;” cf. <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, the Mishnic לאמנה וחוץ לם, beyond the time and place suitable for the thank-offering, חוץ מאחד מהם, excepting one of the same, <hi type="italic">Menachoth</hi> vii. 3, for which the old Heb. would in the first case use בלא, and in the second זולא or מן לבד (= Aram. מן בּר) (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., p. 637). Accordingly ממנו חוץ means <hi type="italic">practer cum </hi>(<hi type="italic">Deum</hi>), <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, unless he will it and make it possible, Old Heb. מבּ, Gen 41:44. <div eID="gen12236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12237" type="x-p"/> In enjoyment man is not free, it depends not on his own will: labour and the enjoyment of it do not stand in a necessary connection; but enjoyment is a gift which God imparts, according as He regards man as good, or as a sinner.
entries.4b413f04e6e2bc46420855847bb9fcafa8bd8208: <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.26">Ecc 2:26</reference> “For to a man who appears to Him as good, He gave wisdom, and knowledge, and joy; but to the sinner He gave the work of gathering and heaping up, in order to give it to him who appears to Him as good: this also is vain, and grasping after the wind;” viz., this striving after enjoyment in and of the labour - it is “vain,” for the purpose and the issue lie far apart; and “striving after the wind,” because that which is striven for, when one thinks that he has it, only too often cannot be grasped, but vanishes into nothing. If we refer this sentence to a collecting and heaping up (Hengst., Grätz, and others), then the author would here come back to what has already been said, and that too in the foregoing section; the reference also to the arbitrary distribution of the good things of life on the part of God (Knobel) is inadmissible, because “this, although it might be called הבל, could not also be called רוח רעות“ (Hitz.); and perfectly inadmissible the reference to the gifts of wisdom, knowledge, and joy (Bullock), for referred to these the sentence gains a meaning only by introducing all kinds of things into the text which here lie out of the connection. <div eID="gen12237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12238" type="x-p"/> Besides, what is here said has indeed a deterministic character, and לפניו, especially if it is thought of in connection with ולח,<note placement="foot">Written with segol under ט in P, <hi type="italic">Biblia Rabb</hi>., and elsewhere. Thus correctly after the Masora, according to which this form of the word has throughout the book <hi type="italic">segol</hi> under ,ט with the single exception of Ecc 7:26. Cf. <hi type="italic">Michol</hi> 124 <hi type="italic">b</hi>, 140 <hi type="italic">b</hi>.</note> sounds as if to the good and the bad their objective worth and distinction should be adjudicated; but this is not the meaning of the author; the unreasonable thought that good or bad is what God’s arbitrary ordinance and judgment stamp it to be, is wholly foreign to him. The “good before Him” is he who appears as good before God, and thus pleases Him, because he is truly good; and the חוטא, placed in contrast, as at <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.26">Ecc 7:26</reference>, is the sinner, not merely such before God, but really such; here לפניו has a different signification than when joined with טוב: one who sins in the sight of God, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, without regarding Him (<reference osisRef="Luke.15.18">Luk 15:18</reference>, ἐνώπιον), serves sin. Regarding ענין, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under 23 <hi type="italic">a</hi>: it denotes a business, <hi type="italic">negotium</hi>; but here such as one fatigues himself with, <hi type="italic">quod negotium facessit</hi>. Among the three charismata, joy stands last, because it is the turning-point of the series of thoughts: joy connected with wise, intelligent activity, is, like wisdom and intelligence themselves, a gift of God. The obj. of לתת (that He may give it) is the store gathered together by the sinner; the thought is the same as that at <reference osisRef="Prov.13.22">Pro 13:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.28.8">Pro 28:8</reference>; Job 27:16. The perfect we have so translated, for that which is constantly repeating itself is here designated by the general expression of a thing thus once for all ordained, and thus always continued.  <chapter eID="Eccl.2"/> <div eID="gen12238" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:head>CHAP. II.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 I Said in mine heart <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Being disappointed of my hopes from Knowledg, I resolved in my own Mind to try another course.</ns0:note>, Go to now, I will prove thee <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">O my Soul I will try whe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther I cannot make thee happy.</ns0:note> with mirth <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">By allowing to my self the free enjoyment of the present and sensible Delights of humane Life.</ns0:note>, therefore enjoy pleasure <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Take thy fill of pleasure, and expect satisfaction thence.</ns0:note>: and behold, this also <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> vanity <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Is vain, and unable to make men happy, because sensible pleasures are mean and unsutable to the noble and heaven-born Soul of Man, and if excessively used, apter to cloy and glut men, than to satisfie them, and are frequently mixed with, and most commonly end in bitterness, as being the great instruments and occasions of sin, and of all its fatal consequences.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 I said of laughter <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Of excessive Mirth, which discovers itself by immoderate Laughter, and other outward gestures.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>It is</ns0:hi> mad <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">This is an act and sign of madness, more fit for fools who know nothing, than for wise men, at least in this sinful, and dangerous, and deplorable state of mankind, which calls for seriousness and sorrow from all conside<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rate persons, in which case it is like the laughter of one in a phren<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />zy. And none but a Fool, or mad-Man, can take satisfaction in such light and frothy Pleasures, or expect Happiness from them.</ns0:note>: and of mirth, What doth it <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">What good doth it? Or how can it make men happy? I challenge all the Epicures in the World to give me a solid and satisfactory Answer.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 1. 17.</ns0:note> I sought in mine heart <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> to draw my flesh with wine.</ns0:note> to give my self unto wine <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">To relax and gratifie my flesh with delicious meats and drinks, Synecdochically expressed by <ns0:hi>Wine</ns0:hi> here, as also <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 9. 2. <ns0:hi>Cant.</ns0:hi> 2. 4. &c. as necessary food is by <ns0:hi>Bread, Amos</ns0:hi> 7. 12. compared with 8. 11.</ns0:note>, (yet acquainting my heart with wisdom <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Yet resolving to use my Wisdom, either 1. To set bounds to my pleasures. Or rather 2. That I might try whether I could not arrive at satisfaction, by mixing Wine and Wisdom together, by using Wine to sweeten and allay the toils of Wisdom, and Wis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom to prevent that destruction which many bring upon them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves by intemperate pleasures whilest they seek for satisfaction, that so I might have the comfort, without the danger and mischief of Pleasures.</ns0:note>) and to lay hold on folly <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">To pursue and addict my self to carnal pleasures, which was my folly.</ns0:note>, till I might see what <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> that good for the sons of men, which they should do under the heaven <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> the number of the days of their life.</ns0:note> all the days of their life <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Till by trying several methods I might find out the true way to Contentment and Satisfaction, during this mortal Life.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 I made me great works <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Magnificent works for my honour and delight.</ns0:note>, I built me houses <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Of which see 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 7. 1, &c. & 9. 15, &c.</ns0:note>, I planted me vineyards <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">See <ns0:hi>Cant.</ns0:hi> 8. 11.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 I made me gardens <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>Paradises,</ns0:hi> or Gardens of Pleasure.</ns0:note> and orchards, and I planted trees in them of all <ns0:hi>kind of</ns0:hi> fruits <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Mixing Pleasure and Profit together.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 I made me pools of water <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Because the Rain there fell but seldom.</ns0:note>, to water therewith the wood that bringeth forth trees <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">The nurseries of young Trees newly planted in the Orchards, which for the multi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tude of them were like a Wood or Forrest.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 I got <ns0:hi>me</ns0:hi> servants and maidens, and had <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> sons of my house.</ns0:note> ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vants born in my house <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Of my Bond-servants, which therefore were a part of my possessions, See 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 10. 1. <ns0:hi>Ezra.</ns0:hi> 2. 55.</ns0:note>; also I had great possessions of great and small cattle, above all that were in Jerusa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lem before me.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Kin. 9. 28. & 10. 10, 14, 21, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> I gathered me also silver and gold, and the pe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />culiar treasure of kings <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Either 1. Vast Riches, answerable to the State of a King. Or 2 The greatest Jewels and ra<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ities of other Kings, which they gave to me either as a Tribute, or by way of Present: of which see 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 4. 21. & 9. 11. & 10. 2, 10.</ns0:note>, and of the provinces <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Which were imposed upon or presented by all the Provinces of my Dominions.</ns0:note>: I gat me men-singers and women-singers <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Whose voices were more sweet than the Mens.</ns0:note>, and the de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lights of the sons of men <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Either 1. All other delightful things. Or 2. That in which men generally delight, to wit, <ns0:hi>musical instruments,</ns0:hi> as it follows.</ns0:note>, as <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>musical instruments,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>a choice woman and choice wo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />men.</ns0:hi> Gr. <ns0:hi>men and women cup-bearers.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> musical instruments, and that of all sorts.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:546" />9 So I was great <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">In Riches, and Power, and Glory.</ns0:note>, and increased more than all that were before me in Jerusalem; also my wisdom remain<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed with me <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">As yet I was not whol<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly besotted and seduced from God by these things, as I was after<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wards. I still had the use of my Reason, whereby I was capable of searching after and finding satisfaction, if it was to be had in those things.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 And whatsoever mine eyes desired <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Whatsoever was grateful to my Senses, or my Heart desired. He ascribes desire to the <ns0:hi>Eyes,</ns0:hi> because the sight of the Eyes is the usual and powerful incentive of Desires; of which see <ns0:hi>Ios.</ns0:hi> 7. 21. <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 31. 1. <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 5. 28.</ns0:note>, I kept not from them <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">I denied my self nothing, at least of law<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ful delights, but went to the very utmost bounds of them: which was the occasion of his falling afterward into sinful pleasures.</ns0:note>, I with-held not my heart from any joy <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">As my Heart was vehemently set upon Pleasure, so I did not resist or curb it therein, but made all possible provisions to gratifie it.</ns0:note>: for my heart rejoiced in all my labour <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">I had the comfort of all my Labours, and was not hindred from the free and full enjoyment of them by Sickness or War, or any other calamitous occurrent.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 3. 22. & 5. 18. & 9. 9.</ns0:note> this was my portion of my labour <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">This present and temporary enjoyment of them, was all the benefit which I could expect or receive from all my Labours. So that I made the best of them, I had an heart to use them, which many men through Covetousness have not, and I tasted the sweetness of them, which many others cannot do; and therefore if any man could arrive at happiness by this means, I had done it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 Then I looked on all the works that my hands had wrought, and on the labour that I had laboured to do <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">I made a serious review of my former works and labours, and considered whether I had obtained that satisfaction in them which I designed and expected.</ns0:note>: and behold, all <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 1. 3, 14.</ns0:note> vanity and vexati<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on of spirit; and <ns0:hi>there was</ns0:hi> no <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> excellency.</ns0:note> profit <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">The pleasure was past and gone, and I was never the better for it, but as empty as before, and had nothing left but sorrowful reflections upon it.</ns0:note> under the sun. <ns0:note place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>k</ns0:hi> I found my self suddenly disappointed and wholly dissatisfied in this course.</ns0:note>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 And I turned my self to behold wisdom, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 1. 13. & 7. 25.</ns0:note> and madness, and folly <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Of which see <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 1. 17. Being frustrated of my hopes in plea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sure, I returned to a second and more serious consideration of my first choice, to see whether there was not more satisfaction to be gotten from wisdom, than what I discovered at my first view.</ns0:note>: for what <ns0:hi>can</ns0:hi> the man <ns0:hi>do</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">To find out the truth in this matter, to discover the utmost sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tisfaction which was possibly to be found in pleasures. So this is added as a reason why he gave over the thoughts of Pleasures, and directed them to another object, and why he so confidently assert<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed their vanity from his own particular Experience, because he had made the best of them, and it was a vain thing for any private <ns0:hi>man</ns0:hi> to expect that from them which could not be found by a <ns0:hi>King,</ns0:hi> and such a King, who had so much Wisdom to invent, and such vast Riches to pursue and enjoy all imaginable delights, and who had made it his design and business to search this to the bottom.</ns0:note> that cometh after the king <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">That succeeds me in this enquiry.</ns0:note>? <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> in those things which have been al<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ready done.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>even</ns0:hi> that which hath been already done <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">As by others in former times, so especially by my self. They can make no new discove<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ries as to this point.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 Then I saw <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>Yet I saw.</ns0:hi> For this is added to prevent an Objection or mistake.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>that there is an ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cellency in wis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom more than in folly,</ns0:hi> &c.</ns0:note> that wisdom excelleth folly <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Although Wisdom is not sufficient to make men tru<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly and perfectly happy, yet it is of a far greater use and excellency than vain Pleasures, or any other follies.</ns0:note>, as far as light excelleth darkness <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Vastly and un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />speakable. Light is very pleasant and comfortable, and withal of great necessity, and singular use to discover the differences of persons and things, to prevent mistakes and dangers, and to direct all a mans paths in the right way, whereas Darkness is in itself doleful, and leads men into innumerable Confusions, and Errours, and Miseries.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Pro. 17. 24. Ch. 8. 1.</ns0:note> The wise mans eyes <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> in his head <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">In their proper place, and therefore they can see, which they could not do if they were out of his head. He hath the use of his Eyes and Reason, and sees his way, and orders all his af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fairs with discretion, and foresees, and so avoids many dangers and mischiefs.</ns0:note>, but the fool walketh in darkness <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Manageth his affairs ignorantly, rashly, and foolishly, whereby he sheweth that his Eyes are not in his head, but in his heels, or as it is expressed, <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 17. 24. <ns0:hi>in the ends of the earth.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>: and <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>Yet,</ns0:hi> notwithstanding this excellency of Wisdom a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bove folly, for our conduct in the matters of this Life, yet at last they both come to one end.</ns0:note> I my self perceived also, that <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ps. 49. 10. Ch. 9. 2, 3.</ns0:note> one event happeneth unto them all <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Both are subject to the same cala<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mities, and to death itself which utterly takes away all difference between them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 Then said I in my heart, As it happeneth to the fool, so it <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> happen <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> to me, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> to me.</ns0:note> happeneth even to me; and why was I then <ns0:hi>more</ns0:hi> wise <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">What benefit have I by my Wisdom? Or, To what purpose did I desire and take so much pains for Wisdom?</ns0:note>? Then I said in my heart, That this also <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> vanity.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 For <ns0:hi>there is</ns0:hi> no remembrance of the wise more than of the fool for ever <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Their Name and Memory, though it may flourish for a season among some men, yet it will not last for ever, but will in a little time be worn out, as we see in most of the wise men of <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> ages, whose very Names, together with all their Monuments, are utterly lost, as hath been oft observed and bewailed by learned Writers in several Ages.</ns0:note>; seeing that which now <ns0:hi>is,</ns0:hi> in the days to come shall all be forgotten: and how dieth the wise <ns0:hi>man?</ns0:hi> as the fool <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">He must die as certainly as the fool, and after death be as little remembred and honoured.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17 Therefore I hated life <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">My Life, though accompanied with so much Honour, and Plea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sure, and Wisdom, was a burden to me, and I was apt to wish ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther that I had never been born, or that I might speedily die.</ns0:note>, because the work that is wrought under the sun <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> grievous unto me <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">All humane designs and works are so far from yielding me that satisfaction which I expected, that the consideration of them en<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />creaseth my discontent.</ns0:note>: for all <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> vanity and vexation of spirit.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 Yea, I hated all my labour, which I had <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> labour<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed.</ns0:note> taken under the sun <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">All these Riches, and Buildings, and other fruits of my la<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bour, were the matter of my Repentance, and aggravations of my Misery.</ns0:note>: because <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ps. 49. 10.</ns0:note> I should leave it unto the man that shall be after me <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Because I must, and that everlastingly, part with them, and leave them all behind me.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19 And who knoweth whether he shall be a wise <ns0:hi>man</ns0:hi> or a fool <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Who will undo all that I have done, and turn the effects of my Wisdom into instruments of his Folly, and occasions of ruine. Some think he had such an Opinion of <ns0:hi>Rehoboam.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>? yet shall he have rule over all my la<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bour wherein I have laboured, and wherein I have shewed my self wise under the sun. This <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> also va<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nity.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20 Therefore I went about to cause my heart to despair <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">I gave my self up to despondency, and despair of ever reaping that satisfaction which I promised to my self.</ns0:note> of all the labour which I took under the sun.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21 For there is a man whose labour <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> in wisdom, and in knowledg, and in equity <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Who useth great Industry, and Prudence, and Justice too in the management of his affairs, and therefore might as confidently expect Gods blessing, and the comfort of his labours, as any other man.</ns0:note>: yet to a man that hath not laboured therein <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">So as I have done: who hath spent his days in sloth and folly.</ns0:note>, shall he <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> gi<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>t..</ns0:note> leave it <ns0:hi>for</ns0:hi> his portion. This also <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> vanity, and a great evil <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">A great disorder in itself, and a great disgrace to this World, and a great torment to a considering mind.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 1. 3. & 3. 9.</ns0:note> For what hath man <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">What comfort or benefit remains to any man after this short and frail Life is once ended? Or, what advantage hath he by all his labours above him who never laboured, and yet enjoyeth all the fruits of his labours.</ns0:note> of all his labour, and of the vexation of his heart wherein he hath laboured under the sun?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">23 For all his days <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Job 14. 1.</ns0:note> sorrows <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>Though all his days</ns0:hi> were <ns0:hi>sorrows, i. e.</ns0:hi> full of sorrows. For this seems added to aggravate the evil mentioned in the foregoing verse. Though he took great and unwearied pains all his days, yet after death he hath no more benefit by it than another man hath.</ns0:note>, and his travel grief <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">The toils of his Body are, or were, accompanied with the vexa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tions of his Mind.</ns0:note>; yea, his heart taketh not rest in the night <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Either because his mind is distracted, and his <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>leep broken with perplexing cares and fears.</ns0:note>. This is also vanity.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:546" />24 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">

                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>. 3. 12, 13, 12. & 5. 18. 28. 15.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>There is</ns0:hi> nothing better for a man <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Or, Is there <ns0:hi>any thing better for a man?</ns0:hi> Which implies that there is nothing better, to wit, for mans present comfort and sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tisfaction; this is the chief, and indeed the only considerable benefit of his labours.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>than</ns0:hi> that he should eat and drink, and <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> he <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>, <ns0:hi>
                           <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap> 
                           <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> should make his soul enjoy good <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">That he should thankfully take, and freely and chearfully enjoy the comforts which God gives him.</ns0:note> in all his labour. This also I saw that it <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> from the hand of God <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">That this also is a singular gift of God, and not to be procured by a mans own Wis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom or Diligence.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">25 For who can eat <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Who can more freely and fully enjoy the Comforts of this Life than I did? This verse is added to confirm what he said in the foregoing verse from his own Experience, which was the more considerable, because no man ever was a more capable Judg of these matters, none could either have more Creature-comforts, or more addict himself to the enjoyment of them, or improve them to better advantage than he did, and therefore he could best tell what was the greatest good to be found in them, and whether they were able of themselves, without Gods special gift, to yield a man satisfaction.</ns0:note>, or who else can hasten <ns0:hi>here<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />unto</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">To wit, to the procuring and enjoying of them. Who can pursue them with more diligence, or obtain them with more speed and readiness, or embrace them with more greediness and alacrity?</ns0:note> more than I?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="26">26 For <ns0:hi>God</ns0:hi> giveth to a man that <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> good <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">

                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> in his sight <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Who not only seems to be good to Men, as many bad Men do, but is really and sincerely good.                            </ns0:gap>s.</ns0:hi> 7. 26. and oft elsewhere.
